title: RBI's Foreign Currency Deposit Scheme Pulls in $20.7 Billion as NRIs Rush to Lock In 6.75% Dollar Returns
excerpt: The central bank's FCNR swap facility, designed to bolster India's foreign exchange reserves, has attracted billions from NRI depositors drawn by tax-free returns and favourable exchange rates.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • RBI's FCNR scheme attracted $20.7 billion in five weeks, with $17.4 billion from FCNR(B) deposits.
  • Banks offer 6.75% annual interest on US dollar deposits, significantly higher than US fixed deposit rates.
  • The scheme runs until September 30, 2026, with potential inflows estimated at $30 billion to $80 billion.
  • FCNR deposits are tax-free for NRIs and carry no currency conversion risk, enhancing their appeal.

  • The RBI's FCNR swap facility has attracted $20.7 billion as of July 17, with FCNR(B) deposits accounting for $17.4 billion of the total
  • Banks are offering approximately 6.75% annual interest on US dollar deposits with 3-5 year tenures — significantly above comparable US fixed deposits
  • The scheme runs from June 8 to September 30, 2026, with state-run banks estimating total inflows could reach $30 billion
  • FCNR deposits carry a one-year lock-in, are tax-free in India for NRIs, and carry no currency conversion risk as both deposit and withdrawal are in the same foreign currency

India's Reserve Bank has pulled off a quiet financial coup. Its Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposit scheme, launched on June 8 as a measure to shore up India's foreign exchange reserves, has attracted $20.7 billion in just over five weeks — with the strongest inflows coming from NRIs in the UAE, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

The Mechanics

Under the scheme, Indian banks are authorised to accept foreign currency deposits from NRIs at competitive interest rates. The current benchmark is approximately 6.75% per annum on US dollar deposits with 3-5 year tenures — a rate that significantly exceeds what NRIs can earn on dollar fixed deposits at US banks, where rates have been falling as the Federal Reserve eases monetary policy.

https://x.com/RBI/status/2079190423927767519

Of the $20.7 billion attracted through the RBI's swap window, FCNR(B) deposits account for $17.4 billion. The scheme runs through September 30, 2026, and state-run banks have projected total inflows could reach $30 billion by the deadline. Bank of America's more bullish estimate suggests India could attract as much as $80 billion if current trends hold.

Why NRIs Are Piling In

The appeal is straightforward: FCNR deposits are denominated in foreign currency (USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, CAD, or AUD), so there is no currency conversion risk for NRIs who earn and spend in those currencies. Interest income is tax-free in India under current regulations for non-resident depositors. And the rates being offered — particularly on the dollar — are meaningfully above alternatives.

Why NRIs Are Investing
›No currency conversion risk for NRIs.
›Interest income is tax-free in India.
›Higher rates than US dollar fixed deposits.
›Minimum tenure of one year, maximum of five.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=UadSIU_F8J4

The minimum tenure is one year, with a maximum of five years. Early withdrawal is permitted after the lock-in period, though at a penalty rate. Banks are offering the highest rates on 3-year and 5-year tenures, where they have the most room to deploy the funds domestically.

"This is essentially a risk-free dollar play for NRIs — you're getting Indian bank rates on dollar deposits with no currency risk and no Indian tax liability."

— Banking analyst, quoted in LiveMint

What the RBI Gets

For the RBI, the scheme serves a dual purpose: it bolsters India's foreign exchange reserves at a time of global currency volatility, and it provides Indian banks with stable foreign currency funding that reduces their dependence on volatile short-term external borrowing. The central bank offers participating banks a concessional swap facility, effectively subsidising the higher deposit rates.

What NRIs Should Know

While the returns are attractive, NRIs should be aware of several fine points. FCNR deposits are subject to FDIC-equivalent protection under India's Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), which covers up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank — a relatively low ceiling for large dollar deposits. The tax treatment may also differ in the NRI's country of residence; US-based NRIs, for instance, must report FCNR interest income on their US tax returns regardless of its Indian tax-free status.

NRIs interested in the scheme should act before the September 30 deadline, as banks may tighten rates as they approach their internal deposit targets.
